title: Arithmetic Slices II - Subsequence
description:
# Arithmetic Slices II - Subsequence

Given an integer array `nums`, return the number of arithmetic subsequences in `nums`.

An arithmetic subsequence must satisfy all of the following:

* it uses at least three elements;
* it keeps the original relative order of the chosen elements;
* the difference between every two consecutive chosen elements is the same.

The subsequence does not need to be contiguous. For example, `[2, 6, 10]` is a subsequence of `[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]` and is arithmetic with difference `4`.

Count choices of indices separately, even when they produce equal values. The final answer fits in a signed 32-bit integer.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [2,4,6,8,10]
**Output:** 7
**Explanation:** The arithmetic subsequences are `[2,4,6]`, `[4,6,8]`, `[6,8,10]`, `[2,4,6,8]`, `[4,6,8,10]`, `[2,4,6,8,10]`, and `[2,6,10]`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [7,7,7,7,7]
**Output:** 16
**Explanation:** Every subsequence with length at least 3 is arithmetic.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= nums.length <= 1000`
*   `-2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1`

tests.description: all equal values produce every length-at-least-three subsequence
zero-difference combinations for four equal values
four-term progression contributes triples and quadruple
duplicate middle value creates overlapping subsequence choices
geometric growth has no arithmetic subsequence of length three
difference requires long arithmetic to avoid int overflow
several differences share the same array

solutions.name: Per-Index Difference Map DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each index `i`, keep a map from difference `d` to the number of weak arithmetic subsequences of length at least two that end at `i` with difference `d`. For every pair `(j, i)`, the pair itself creates one new weak subsequence, and every weak subsequence ending at `j` with the same difference becomes a valid length-at-least-three subsequence when `nums[i]` is appended.

## Key Insight

Counting length-at-least-two sequences avoids special-casing triples. `dp[j][d]` is exactly the number of sequences that become complete answers after adding `nums[i]`, while `dp[j][d] + 1` is added into `dp[i][d]` for future extensions.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Global Difference Bucket DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Group all index pairs by their `long` difference first. Then solve each difference independently. Inside one difference bucket, process pairs in increasing right endpoint order and maintain how many weak subsequences with that difference currently end at each index.

## Key Insight

The standard recurrence does not actually require all differences to be mixed together. For a fixed difference, a pair `(j, i)` completes exactly the weak subsequences already ending at `j`, then creates the same number plus the pair itself as weak subsequences ending at `i`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Coordinate-Compressed Difference Arrays
solutions.description:
## Approach

Precompute the distinct incoming differences for each endpoint `i`, assign each such difference a compact slot, and store counts in integer arrays instead of hash maps during the recurrence. The recurrence is the same as the per-index map solution, but the storage shape is explicit and dense per endpoint.

## Key Insight

This version separates key discovery from dynamic programming. It is useful when teaching that the state space is bounded by the `O(n^2)` index pairs, even though the numerical difference values can be huge and sparse.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Last-Two-Index Bottom-Up DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Let `dp[j][i]` be the number of arithmetic subsequences of length at least three whose last two indices are `j` and `i`. For each possible predecessor `k < j` with `nums[k], nums[j], nums[i]` forming one arithmetic step, add `dp[k][j] + 1` into `dp[j][i]`.

## Key Insight

This state says exactly what the last two chosen elements are, so the transition is easy to reason about: every valid predecessor creates a new triple, and every longer sequence ending at `(k, j)` can be extended by `i`. It is slower, but it is a clear bridge to the optimized difference-map recurrence.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^3)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)

solutions.name: Memoized Forward Pair Extension
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat every ordered pair `(i, j)` as the first two elements of a potential arithmetic subsequence. Recursively count all later indices that can continue the same difference. Choosing a next index contributes one completed subsequence immediately, plus all longer continuations from that next pair.

## Key Insight

This top-down direction mirrors the definition of subsequence extension. Memoizing by `(lastIndex, difference)` prevents recomputing the same suffix extension tree for every earlier start pair.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^3)
- Space Complexity: O(n^2)
